transcript:
Meeting: Acorn Financial — Enterprise check-in (SDK upgrade + retries/timeouts migration)
Date: 2026-02-06
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Dev Patel (Customer Support/CS), Ibrahim Khan (SDKs TL), Sabrina James (Python SDK), Wei Chen (Docs)
Acorn Financial: Rachel Kim (Platform Eng), Thomas Reed (SRE), Priya Nair (Security), Miguel Alvarez (Backend)

Summary (auto-generated)
- Acorn is planning to upgrade Redwood SDKs (TS + Python) to pick up standardized auth/env var precedence, retry/backoff behavior (incl. Retry-After), and the updated timeout model.
- Team discussed safe retry patterns for streaming and the need to avoid duplicate side effects/billing concerns.
- Acorn requested clearer docs on: per-request timeout configuration for streaming, how “overall timeout” behaves, and what errors are retryable vs terminal.
- Redwood agreed to add a migration doc callout for corporate proxy streaming disconnects and recommended defaults.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Current production symptoms (429 spikes, timeouts, stream disconnects)
2) SDK versioning + migration impact
3) Retry policy defaults (429/5xx/network) and Retry-After
4) Timeout model (connect/read/overall) and how it maps in TS/Python
5) Streaming semantics: partial output, disconnect errors, and conservative retry guidance
6) Logging fields: request_id, retry_count, timeout_ms, disconnect_reason

Action items (auto-generated)
- Dev (Redwood): Send migration notes + config examples for TS and Python (today)
- Wei (Redwood): Add docs clarification re: streaming timeout + proxy disconnect note (draft by next week)
- Rachel (Acorn): Pilot TS SDK upgrade in staging and confirm retry/timeout behavior (by Feb 11)
- Thomas (Acorn): Provide sample request_ids for two streaming disconnect incidents (by Feb 11)

Transcript

[00:00] Dev Patel: Alright, I think we’re good. Hi everyone—Rachel, Thomas, Priya, Miguel—thanks for making time. Goal today is basically to walk through the SDK upgrade and migration, and make sure retries and timeouts are tuned the way you expect. And Wei’s here to capture doc gaps.

[00:18] Rachel Kim: Sounds good.

[00:20] Dev Patel: Quick intros on our side—Dev, I’m in CS/support. Ibrahim is our SDK tech lead. Sabrina owns Python SDK and examples. Wei is docs. 

[00:30] Ibrahim Khan: Hey.

[00:31] Sabrina James: Hi everyone.

[00:33] Wei Chen: Hello.

[00:35] Dev Patel: And if it’s okay, we’ll spend like ten minutes on your current issues, then go into “what changes” and recommended settings.

[00:44] Thomas Reed: Yep.

[00:46] Dev Patel: Cool. Rachel, do you want to summarize what’s prompting the upgrade? I saw the notes about 429 handling and streaming disconnects.

[00:55] Rachel Kim: Yeah. We have two services. One is TypeScript, one is Python. The TS one seemed to behave… more predictably when we hit rate limits. Python, we had cases where streaming calls kind of hang, or the timeout didn’t fire when we expected. Also we’re behind a corporate proxy for one environment. So we’re trying to get onto the versions where you’ve standardized everything.

[01:19] Dev Patel: Got it. That matches what we’ve been seeing across customers. Thomas, from SRE perspective, what are you seeing—timeouts, retries, or load spikes?

[01:28] Thomas Reed: The big one is when we get elevated 429s, the client behavior matters. We’ve had “retry storms” in the past with other vendors. We want to respect Retry-After. And we also need to ensure we’re not retrying requests that could cause duplicate downstream actions. We mostly do read-only generation, but some flows do create tickets or write to a DB after generation.

[01:53] Dev Patel: Makes sense. Priya, anything on security side that’s blocking upgrades?

[01:57] Priya Nair: Mostly we need confirmation on environment variables and secret handling. We don’t want API keys showing up in logs when debug is on. And we want clear precedence rules so engineers don’t accidentally pull the wrong key from the environment.

[02:12] Dev Patel: Totally. That’s part of what changed.

[02:15] Miguel Alvarez: And I have one more: In TS we had a concern that it was retrying on 400 at one point, or at least it looked like it. That made finance nervous about duplicate billing. So I want to be very clear what gets retried.

[02:29] Ibrahim Khan: Yep, we can cover that. That was one of the specific mismatches we fixed—classification and error taxonomy.

[02:37] Dev Patel: Great. Let’s move into upgrade overview. Ibrahim, can you give the “what’s standard now” elevator pitch?

[02:44] Ibrahim Khan: Sure. Across Python/TS/Go we now align on four things: auth resolution order, retry policy defaults including Retry-After parsing, timeout model (connect/read/overall semantics), and streaming behavior—specifically what happens on disconnect, partial output, and what we recommend for retries. Also, errors now consistently include request_id and a retryable flag.

[03:08] Rachel Kim: When you say “auth resolution order,” that’s like explicit key in code versus env var?

[03:13] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. The standard is: explicit parameter in client constructor wins, then environment variables (new canonical names), and we’re deprecating old env var names with warnings.

[03:25] Priya Nair: What are the canonical env vars?

[03:28] Sabrina James: For the main API key we’re standardizing on something like REDWOOD_API_KEY. Some languages historically used REDWOOD_TOKEN or REDWOOD_KEY; those are being deprecated. And if you pass api_key directly, env is ignored.

[03:43] Priya Nair: And no printing the value in errors, right?

[03:46] Sabrina James: Correct. Error messages will say like “missing API key; set REDWOOD_API_KEY” but won’t echo the key. Debug logging redacts it.

[03:56] Wei Chen: Priya, I’m noting we should make the doc explicit: “SDK never logs full secrets, even with debug enabled,” and show the redaction behavior.

[04:05] Priya Nair: Yes please.

[04:07] Dev Patel: Let’s talk retries—Miguel’s 400 concern. Ibrahim?

[04:11] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah. Default retries are only for a limited set: 429 rate limited, certain 5xx server errors, and network/transient errors (connection reset, timeouts at transport layer). We do NOT retry 400, 401, 403, 404, 422, etc. And we specifically classify 408/409 carefully—by default, we treat 408 as retryable in some clients, but we’re standardizing the list.

[04:37] Miguel Alvarez: So 400 is never retried. That’s good.

[04:39] Ibrahim Khan: Right. If you saw that, it may have been a middleware bug where errors were misclassified. That’s fixed in the refactor.

[04:47] Thomas Reed: Can you confirm how you handle Retry-After? We’ve seen providers send date format versus seconds.

[04:54] Ibrahim Khan: We parse both formats: either integer seconds or HTTP-date. The SDK will wait at least that long before retrying, plus a small jitter to avoid herd behavior.

[05:07] Thomas Reed: And if Retry-After is missing?

[05:09] Ibrahim Khan: Then we fall back to exponential backoff with jitter. The defaults are tuned to be conservative—so you won’t hammer immediately.

[05:19] Rachel Kim: “Conservative” meaning… what max attempts?

[05:22] Ibrahim Khan: Defaults are something like max 3 attempts total for non-streaming requests. The exact number depends on endpoint, but the standard is: a small cap, and we surface configuration to change it.

[05:34] Thomas Reed: Okay. We’d likely keep it low.

[05:36] Dev Patel: On timeouts—this was the main pain for Python streaming. Sabrina, do you want to explain what changed?

[05:44] Sabrina James: Yep. Previously, Python streaming had cases where user-specified timeouts weren’t applied consistently—especially if the stream started and then stalled. Now we have an explicit timeout model: connect timeout, read timeout, and optionally overall timeout. For streaming, “read timeout” is the important one: it’s basically “how long we’ll wait without receiving bytes.” Overall timeout can be tricky for long streams.

[06:12] Rachel Kim: This is exactly where we got confused. We set “timeout=30” expecting the whole request to end after 30 seconds, but streaming outputs can run longer than that.

[06:22] Sabrina James: Right. So we’re updating docs to recommend: for streaming, set a longer overall (or disable overall) and use read timeout to catch stalls. For non-streaming, overall timeout is fine.

[06:35] Thomas Reed: In TS, how is this represented? Fetch doesn’t really have connect/read as separate, right?

[06:41] Ibrahim Khan: Correct. In TS we expose an overall request timeout via AbortController, and for streaming we implement a “stall timeout” pattern that aborts if no chunks arrive within N ms. That approximates read timeout.

[06:56] Rachel Kim: That’s good. Is the name “timeout_ms” the same across languages?

[07:01] Ibrahim Khan: We aligned naming in docs and config as much as possible, but there are language idioms. We do standardize the semantics and the doc page will map “overall/connect/read.” Wei’s capturing the naming confusion, I think.

[07:14] Wei Chen: Yes. I’ll add a table: TS “timeoutMs” and “streamStallTimeoutMs” vs Python “connect_timeout”, “read_timeout”, “timeout” (overall).

[07:27] Miguel Alvarez: On streaming disconnects behind proxy—what’s the recommended behavior? Our proxy sometimes buffers, then the stream ends abruptly.

[07:37] Dev Patel: We’ve heard that. We’re making SDKs surface a typed error with request_id and a disconnect reason when possible.

[07:45] Sabrina James: In Python, if the connection closes mid-chunk, you’ll get a specific StreamingDisconnectError (name approximate) that includes request_id if we received it, and it also includes whether partial output was received.

[07:59] Rachel Kim: Partial output meaning we still get tokens we got so far?

[08:02] Sabrina James: Exactly. The iterator yields what it has; if it breaks, we raise the typed exception. The app can decide whether to display partial output or treat it as failure.

[08:12] Thomas Reed: And should we retry automatically?

[08:14] Ibrahim Khan: We do not auto-retry streaming by default. That’s deliberate to avoid duplicate side effects and weird UX. We recommend: if you want retries, do it at the application layer with an idempotency key, and only for safe operations.

[08:30] Miguel Alvarez: Does Redwood support idempotency keys?

[08:33] Dev Patel: The platform supports request IDs and we have guidance on idempotency—some endpoints accept an idempotency key header. We’ll follow up with exact header name for your endpoints.

[08:44] Priya Nair: Is that header sensitive? Any logging concerns?

[08:47] Ibrahim Khan: It’s not a secret generally, but we still recommend not logging full headers unless necessary. The SDK can log a hashed or truncated version if needed.

[08:58] Priya Nair: Okay.

[09:00] Dev Patel: Let’s get more concrete with your planned rollout. Rachel, which services and which SDK versions are you targeting?

[09:07] Rachel Kim: We’re on redwood-sdk-typescript 0.18-ish, and Python 0.9-ish. We plan to go to whatever includes the standardized retry/timeouts. We can do TS first because it’s lower risk.

[09:22] Ibrahim Khan: Great. The versions you want are the ones after the retry middleware refactor and timeout updates. We’ll send you the exact minimum versions. 

[09:32] Miguel Alvarez: Are there breaking changes? Like constructor params renamed?

[09:36] Ibrahim Khan: Minimal breaking. Mostly additive. The main thing is env var names—old ones still work but with deprecation warnings. And timeout defaults might change slightly to be consistent.

[09:49] Thomas Reed: What are the new defaults?

[09:52] Ibrahim Khan: For non-streaming, overall timeout is set to a sane production default—enough for typical generations, but not infinite. For streaming, the key is stall/read timeout. We can recommend values based on your typical completion length.

[10:10] Thomas Reed: Our typical streams are 30–90 seconds depending on user prompt.

[10:14] Sabrina James: Then you probably want overall timeout 2–3 minutes, and read timeout maybe 20–30 seconds (meaning if nothing arrives for 20–30 seconds, abort).

[10:27] Rachel Kim: That would have prevented some hangs we saw.

[10:31] Dev Patel: On observability, we’re also standardizing logging fields. Thomas, what do you need emitted?

[10:37] Thomas Reed: request_id is huge. Also retry_count, and the final status code. For streaming, disconnect reason.

[10:45] Ibrahim Khan: Yes—SDK errors include request_id and retry attempt count. In success cases, we also expose request_id via response metadata.

[10:54] Miguel Alvarez: In TS, is request_id on the response headers?

[10:57] Ibrahim Khan: Yes, and we propagate it into the returned object. For streaming, each event can include it or we include it in the stream wrapper.

[11:08] Rachel Kim: We should standardize that in our internal interface.

[11:11] Dev Patel: Wei, this seems like a doc ask: “how to get request_id in each language.”

[11:16] Wei Chen: Yep, I’ll add code snippets showing “print(response.requestId)” or equivalent.

[11:22] Priya Nair: And confirm it’s okay to log request_id. It’s not PII, right?

[11:26] Dev Patel: Correct, it’s an internal tracing ID. We recommend logging it for support.

[11:33] Thomas Reed: Back to retries—what about 500 vs 502 vs 503? All retryable?

[11:39] Ibrahim Khan: Generally: 500, 502, 503, 504 are retryable. 501 not. And 429 retryable, respecting Retry-After. If the platform returns a structured error code indicating terminal, we won’t retry.

[11:55] Miguel Alvarez: Structured error code meaning like an enum?

[11:58] Ibrahim Khan: Yes. We’re standardizing error codes so SDKs can classify without guessing from message strings.

[12:07] Rachel Kim: Great.

[12:09] Dev Patel: Let’s hit streaming and billing concerns. Miguel, you mentioned finance. What’s the exact worry—duplicate billing due to retry?

[12:17] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah. If the client retries after partial output, could we be billed twice for tokens? And also, if our app does something after receiving output, could it double-trigger.

[12:30] Dev Patel: On the platform side, token billing is per request. If you retry, it’s a new request, so yes it can generate additional tokens. That’s why we say streaming retries are app-level and conservative.

[12:44] Ibrahim Khan: And that’s why the SDK doesn’t automatically replay a stream. If you choose to, you can implement “resume” by reissuing with the same prompt, but it’s not guaranteed to match. We’ll document: avoid automatic retries for streams unless you have idempotency protection and are okay with extra tokens.

[13:05] Thomas Reed: That’s an important callout. Put it in bold.

[13:07] Wei Chen: Noted.

[13:09] Priya Nair: Also for regulated environment, if we need to prove we didn’t log secrets—do you have guidance for safe debug logs?

[13:18] Sabrina James: In Python, debug mode logs request metadata but redacts auth headers. Same in Go and TS. If you attach a custom logger, we recommend a redaction filter.

[13:33] Priya Nair: Okay.

[13:35] Dev Patel: Rachel, do you want to walk through your current configuration? Like what are you setting today?

[13:40] Rachel Kim: In TS we set retries=5 (maybe too high), timeout=30_000, and we don’t have a stall timeout. In Python we set a global timeout to 30 and hoped it applied.

[13:54] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah, that’s a common setup but not ideal for streaming. I’d suggest TS retries maybe 2 or 3 max, and separate streaming stall timeout.

[14:07] Thomas Reed: Also, for 429 we’d prefer longer waits rather than many attempts.

[14:11] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly—Retry-After will dominate. More attempts doesn’t help if you’re quota-limited.

[14:20] Dev Patel: What about backoff jitter—do you need deterministic for tests?

[14:24] Miguel Alvarez: We have integration tests that assume no sleep. If jitter is on, tests can slow.

[14:31] Ibrahim Khan: We expose a way to inject a “sleep” function or disable actual waiting in tests. In TS you can pass a retryDelay override; in Python you can set a transport option. We’ll send a snippet.

[14:47] Rachel Kim: That would be helpful.

[14:49] Wei Chen: I’ll add a “testing retries” section in migration notes.

[14:54] Dev Patel: Nice. Let’s discuss the actual migration steps for you.

[14:58] Ibrahim Khan: Step one: update env vars. If you’re using legacy names, set the new ones and remove old over time. Step two: upgrade TS SDK, confirm request_id logging and retry_count. Step three: update timeout config: set overall timeout for non-streaming, set streaming stall timeout. Step four: for Python, use connect/read/overall explicitly.

[15:22] Rachel Kim: For env vars, we currently use REDWOOD_TOKEN in one environment.

[15:27] Sabrina James: That will still work but you’ll see a warning. We recommend switching to REDWOOD_API_KEY.

[15:34] Priya Nair: Warnings in logs are okay, but we need to track them so they don’t trigger alerts.

[15:39] Dev Patel: Understood. We can suggest filtering those or moving quickly to the new env var.

[15:45] Thomas Reed: On Python, can you explain how read timeout behaves if tokens are coming slowly? Like every 10 seconds.

[15:53] Sabrina James: Read timeout is “time between bytes/chunks.” So if you’re receiving something every 10 seconds, and read timeout is 20 seconds, you’re fine. If proxy buffers and you get nothing for 30 seconds, it times out.

[16:10] Thomas Reed: That’s what we want.

[16:12] Miguel Alvarez: In TS, if the stream is alive but quiet, does your stall timeout reset per chunk?

[16:18] Ibrahim Khan: Yes. It’s essentially a watchdog timer that resets when a chunk/event arrives.

[16:24] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[16:26] Dev Patel: Let’s pause—any concerns about rollout risk? We can talk about staging, canary.

[16:32] Rachel Kim: We’ll do staging for a week. We can also canary 5% of traffic.

[16:37] Thomas Reed: And we’ll watch 429 rates and client retry rates.

[16:41] Dev Patel: Great. Redwood side, we have dashboards for SDK retry/timeout metrics if you opt into logging fields; but at minimum, if you can share request_id on incidents, we can trace.

[16:54] Priya Nair: Are you collecting telemetry automatically?

[16:58] Dev Patel: Not automatically without explicit opt-in. By default it’s just client-side logging you control.

[17:04] Priya Nair: Good.

[17:06] Wei Chen: Another doc gap question: do you want a quick decision tree in docs? Like “If you’re doing streaming, don’t set overall timeout too low; set stall timeout.”

[17:16] Rachel Kim: Yes. That would prevent confusion.

[17:19] Dev Patel: We can do that.

[17:21] Miguel Alvarez: Another nuance: we use both hosted API and dedicated capacity. Do the retry semantics differ?

[17:28] Ibrahim Khan: Semantics are the same from SDK perspective. But you may see different patterns of 429. On Dedicated, 429 is usually concurrency limit; hosted can be global rate limit. Either way, Retry-After should be present on 429 now.

[17:47] Thomas Reed: “Should be present” meaning guaranteed?

[17:50] Ibrahim Khan: We’re making it consistent. If it’s absent, we fall back to backoff. But you should see it.

[17:57] Dev Patel: If you don’t, send us the request_id and we’ll verify gateway behavior.

[18:03] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[18:05] Priya Nair: For auth, do you support bearer tokens vs API keys? Some teams use service tokens.

[18:12] Sabrina James: Yes, bearer token auth is supported. The header is “Authorization: Bearer …”. Same precedence rules apply.

[18:20] Priya Nair: And env var name changes apply there too?

[18:24] Sabrina James: We standardize on API key as primary. If you use bearer tokens, we document the env var for that. But we avoid having too many overlapping env vars; we’ll be explicit in docs.

[18:38] Wei Chen: I’ll double-check the naming and make sure the migration page covers both API key and bearer token cases.

[18:45] Dev Patel: Let’s talk errors. When something fails, what shape do you get now?

[18:50] Ibrahim Khan: Cross-language taxonomy: you’ll get status_code (if HTTP), error_code (our enum), message, request_id, and retryable boolean. Also sometimes “retry_after_ms” when applicable.

[19:04] Thomas Reed: That helps for automated handling.

[19:06] Miguel Alvarez: In Python, is it a typed exception class per error type?

[19:10] Sabrina James: Yes—there’s a base RedwoodError, and then subclasses like RateLimitError, TimeoutError, APIConnectionError, and streaming-specific disconnect error. They all include request_id.

[19:24] Rachel Kim: In TS it’s less typed, right?

[19:27] Ibrahim Khan: It’s typed as classes as well, but JS/TS ecosystem is varied. We provide error classes and type guards.

[19:35] Dev Patel: Okay. Let’s address the corporate proxy streaming issue specifically. Miguel, what happens today—do you see FIN mid-chunk, or just “socket hang up”?

[19:47] Miguel Alvarez: In Node it’s usually “socket hang up” or the stream just ends. In Python, sometimes it blocks forever. We think the proxy buffers and the server thinks it’s done.

[20:02] Sabrina James: In Python, with the new read timeout and disconnect detection, it should not block forever. You should either get new chunks, or it times out and raises.

[20:13] Thomas Reed: That’s good. But we need guidance: should we treat that as retryable?

[20:18] Ibrahim Khan: We recommend treat it as “maybe retryable” only if your request is safe and you’re okay with extra tokens. For UX, some customers show partial output and a “connection lost, try again” CTA.

[20:34] Rachel Kim: We can do that.

[20:36] Wei Chen: I’ll add a doc section: “Common enterprise proxy behaviors,” and recommended pattern: partial output + user retry, not silent automatic.

[20:46] Priya Nair: Please avoid wording that sounds like “your proxy is broken” (laughs).

[20:51] Wei Chen: (laughs) Understood—neutral language.

[20:54] Dev Patel: Great. Can we quickly confirm what information you’ll share when you see disconnects? Request IDs, timestamp, SDK version.

[21:03] Thomas Reed: Yes. We can provide request_id and the service logs including retry_count.

[21:08] Dev Patel: Perfect.

[21:10] Rachel Kim: Do you have recommended default retry settings for 429? Like max attempts and max backoff.

[21:16] Ibrahim Khan: Default max attempts is low. You can set max retry delay cap. But for 429, if Retry-After says 60 seconds, we’ll wait 60. We also cap the overall wait so the client doesn’t hang forever.

[21:33] Thomas Reed: What’s the cap?

[21:35] Ibrahim Khan: It depends, but think in minutes, not tens of minutes. We can share the standard and you can override.

[21:44] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[21:46] Miguel Alvarez: One more. In TS, do you retry on DNS failures?

[21:50] Ibrahim Khan: Yes, network errors like DNS resolution failure can be retryable, but we keep it limited. Also, we don’t retry if the request body can’t be re-sent safely (rare in our case).

[22:02] Thomas Reed: Good.

[22:04] Dev Patel: We’re about halfway. I want to make sure we capture your doc feedback. Wei, what are the doc edits you’re hearing?

[22:12] Wei Chen: Four items: (1) A clear migration table of option names across languages (overall vs connect/read vs stall). (2) A strong warning about streaming retries and billing/side-effects. (3) A section for enterprise proxies and how to handle disconnects + partial output. (4) A snippet per language for “how to log request_id, retry_count, timeout_ms.”

[22:38] Rachel Kim: That’s right.

[22:40] Priya Nair: Also mention secret redaction and env var precedence.

[22:44] Wei Chen: Yep, I’ll add that as (5).

[22:47] Dev Patel: Great. Let’s talk implementation details—Rachel, what does your TS call site look like today? High level is fine.

[22:55] Rachel Kim: We create a client with apiKey from env, then call chat.completions.create with stream: true. We attach an AbortController for user cancel, but it wasn’t always working.

[23:10] Ibrahim Khan: The new TS version fixes AbortController plumbing for streaming. Cancellation should cleanly abort the fetch and stop iteration.

[23:19] Miguel Alvarez: That’s helpful.

[23:21] Sabrina James: Python also improved cancellation via context manager / closing the stream explicitly.

[23:28] Thomas Reed: How do you recommend implementing cancel? For example user navigates away.

[23:33] Ibrahim Khan: In TS, abort the controller. In Python, call close() on the stream or cancel the task if you’re using async. We’ll put that in examples.

[23:46] Dev Patel: Another common gotcha: if you cancel a stream, you may still see partial token usage billed. That’s expected because tokens already generated count.

[23:55] Rachel Kim: Understood.

[23:57] Priya Nair: For audit, do you provide audit logs for API key usage?

[24:02] Dev Patel: For Dedicated/Private deployments, yes there are audit log integrations. For hosted, we provide usage analytics and request IDs. That’s slightly outside today, but happy to connect you.

[24:14] Priya Nair: Okay.

[24:16] Dev Patel: Back to retries. Thomas, do you have a policy like “never exceed 2 retries” across your org?

[24:22] Thomas Reed: Usually yes, plus respect Retry-After. And we prefer exponential backoff with jitter. So your defaults sound aligned.

[24:31] Ibrahim Khan: Great.

[24:33] Rachel Kim: Is there any difference in default timeouts between languages? Because that was part of our confusion—TS felt like it timed out, Python didn’t.

[24:42] Sabrina James: Historically yes. Now we’re aligning the defaults. But there are still differences in underlying HTTP libraries, so behavior can’t be bit-for-bit identical. That’s why we publish semantics and conformance tests.

[24:57] Rachel Kim: Okay. As long as it’s documented.

[25:01] Wei Chen: I’ll include a note like: “Defaults are aligned; implementation differs by language runtime. See semantics.”

[25:09] Miguel Alvarez: What about proxies again—if it buffers, stall timeout might trigger even though server is generating. Then user retries and gets double output.

[25:20] Ibrahim Khan: Right. It’s a tradeoff. If the proxy hides bytes, the client can’t tell progress. We suggest increasing stall timeout in that environment or using a different network path for streaming workloads.

[25:33] Thomas Reed: We might route streaming around the proxy.

[25:36] Priya Nair: That requires security exception; but we can explore.

[25:40] Dev Patel: We can help with a “recommended network” note, but we’ll keep it general.

[25:46] Rachel Kim: How do we detect in code whether we got partial output? You mentioned a flag.

[25:51] Sabrina James: In Python, the exception includes the partial text received so far (or the last chunk) depending on how you consume it. In TS, you can accumulate tokens and if an error is thrown mid-iteration you still have what you appended. The error also indicates “stream_interrupted.”

[26:12] Miguel Alvarez: So it’s on us to keep the buffer.

[26:14] Ibrahim Khan: Yes.

[26:16] Dev Patel: We’re coming up on time, but I want to make sure we set you up for success. Rachel, would you be comfortable doing TS staging upgrade next week and then we do a 30-min follow-up?

[26:28] Rachel Kim: Yes. We can do it by Wednesday.

[26:31] Dev Patel: Great.

[26:32] Thomas Reed: If we see increased retry load, what’s the rollback plan? Just pin old version.

[26:38] Dev Patel: Yes, pin old version and/or set retries to zero temporarily. Also we can coordinate on the platform side if there’s a broader 429 event.

[26:47] Thomas Reed: Okay.

[26:49] Priya Nair: I want to ensure docs specify the env var precedence. Like if both old and new env vars set, which wins?

[26:56] Sabrina James: Good question. We prefer the new canonical env var if both are set. And we’ll emit a warning that multiple were set.

[27:06] Priya Nair: Perfect. That’s the safe behavior.

[27:09] Wei Chen: I’ll add that exact scenario to migration notes.

[27:12] Miguel Alvarez: Can we talk about the “Retry-After” units again. If it’s a date, time zones etc.

[27:18] Ibrahim Khan: It’s HTTP-date in GMT. We parse it accordingly. If parsing fails, we ignore and use backoff.

[27:27] Miguel Alvarez: Okay.

[27:29] Dev Patel: Any other open questions?

[27:32] Rachel Kim: Just confirming: You’ll send minimum versions and code snippets.

[27:36] Dev Patel: Yes.
